title: 13 Defendants Arrested on Federal Indictment Charging Them With Stealing More Than $22.5 Million in Consumer Goods from Trains
body: Press Release 13 Defendants Arrested on Federal Indictment Charging Them With Stealing More Than $22.5 Million in Consumer Goods from Trains Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California LOS ANGELES – 13 defendants were arrested today on a 17-count federal indictment charging them with burglarizing at least three dozen trains and stealing more than $22 million worth of Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, and other products, then selling them on the black market, coordinating their thefts via Instagram. “The scale of the theft is staggering. We have charged a crew of 14 in a scheme to steal more than $22.5 million in cargo from at least three dozen freight trains in Southern California,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash.” “This historic indictment, following a 14-month investigation assisted by our Bureau of Investigation, demonstrates the importance of dismantling entire criminal enterprises — from those stealing the cargo to those profiting from its resale,” Los Angeles County Nathan J. Hochman said. “We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market.” The following defendants charged today are expected to make their initial appearances and be arraigned on the indictment this afternoon in United States District Court in downtown Los Angeles: Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, the crew’s leader; Daniel Angel, 38, a.k.a. “Rayo,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s father; Rodolfo Angel, 23, a.k.a. “Rudy” and “Flaco,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s uncle; Jose Luis Angel, 23, a.k.a. “Joe,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s uncle; Donta Hedgeman, 27, a.k.a. “Dret,” of East Los Angeles; Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, of the Historic South-Central neighborhood of Los Angeles; Daniel Garcia, 36, of East Los Angeles; Carlos Robert Estrada, 28, a.k.a. “JD,” of Whittier; Angel Sanchez, 24, a.k.a. “Fluffy,” of Commerce; Ruben Mario Banuelos, 26, a.k.a. “Bubu,” of East Los Angeles; Fredy Marquina, 25, of the Westlake neighborhood of Los Angeles; Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, of the Vermont Square area of South Los Angeles; Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, of East Los Angeles; Ricardo Mares, 32, of the Florence-Firestone area of Los Angeles. The federal grand jury charged all 14 defendants with one count of conspiracy. The indictment further charges 14 counts of theft of interstate railroad cargo and possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and two counts of violence against railroad carriers. According to the indictment, shipping containers with Nike sneakers and other freight routinely enter the United States from international destinations via the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach then are transported by trains operated by carrier companies for further distribution throughout the U.S. From February 2024 to August 2026, Nathan Angel targeted high-value trains traveling through Southern California carrying Nike sneakers and other products, intending to steal them and resell them on the black market. At his direction, Daniel Angel, Rodolfo Angel, Jose Angel, Villegas, Estrada, and Sanchez rented or used trucks and vans to drive burglars to the railroad tracks, where the burglars boarded the trains. These co-defendants also acted as lookouts. Nathan Angel and other co-conspirators pre-determined locations along the tracks to disable the trains. Hedgeman and other co-conspirators then cut the air hoses of the trains, forcing the trains to come to an emergency stop. Daniel Angel, Rodolfo Angel, Jose Angel, Villegas, Estrada, and Sanchez met the train burglars where they had disabled the trains and helped load stolen train cargo into trucks and vans, which they then transported to stash houses, including the residences of Villegas, Garcia, and Daniel Angel. The burglaries occurred on railroad tracks in Pico Rivera, Fullerton, and other locations in Southern California. Nathan Angel alerted Garcia about the type of products that had been stolen from the trains. They would then discuss resale prices for the stolen products. Nathan Angel sent to Marquina, Martinez, and Espinoza photographs of the stolen Nike sneakers and other products, often while the trains were being burglarized. These co-defendants knowingly took the stolen products into their possession. Marquina then contacted potential buyers, including representatives of a business identified in the indictment as  “Company 1,” a sneaker and streetwear resale brand with headquarters in Los Angeles that was not an authorized Nike reseller. Marquina and Martinez sold the stolen Nike sneakers and other products to Company 1, which then sold the stolen products for a profit. From May 2025 to October 2025, Marquina and Martinez sold thousands of pairs of stolen Nike sneakers, many in their original Nike factory cartons, to Company 1 and received from Company 1 a total of approximately $1,081,493 for the stolen Nike products and other stolen items. Espinoza also obtained stolen Nike sneakers and other stolen goods from suppliers, including Nathan Angel. Garcia helped deliver the stolen goods to Espinoza’s residence, where Espinoza stored them. Espinoza advertised the stolen goods to potential buyers, including on social media accounts. He then sold the stolen goods to buyers for a profit. An indictment contains allegations that a defendant has committed a crime. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent until and unless proven guilty in court. If convicted, the defendants would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for the conspiracy count, up to 10 years in federal prison for each theft count, and a statutory maximum sentence of life in federal prison for each violence against railroad cars count. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Los Angeles Police Department Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department, and the California Highway Patrol Cargo Theft Interdiction Program, with assistance from IRS Criminal Investigation, are investigating this matter. Assistant United States Attorney Diane Roldán and Eric Mackie of the Major Crimes Section is prosecuting this case, with assistance from the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office. Contact Shawn Lewis Public Affairs Officer shawn.lewis@usdoj.gov (213) 458-6803 Updated November 19, 2026 Component USAO - California, Central Press Release Number: 26-221

title: Norway Man Pleads Guilty to Burglarizing a Gun Store and Illegally Possessing Firearms
body: Press Release Norway Man Pleads Guilty to Burglarizing a Gun Store and Illegally Possessing Firearms Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maine Grover Lee Harmon stole 12 firearms PORTLAND, Maine: A Norway man pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in Portland to stealing firearms from a federally licensed firearms dealer and being a felon in possession of a firearm. According to court records, in March 2026, 12 handguns were stolen from J&K Sporting Goods in West Paris, a federally licensed firearms dealer. In April 2026, Grover Lee Harmon , 41, was arrested on unrelated warrants during a traffic stop. A search of Harmon’s vehicle revealed three pistol magazines. Investigators subsequently executed a search warrant at a residence used by Harmon and his girlfriend and located two of the firearms stolen in the March burglary. During an interview with investigators, Harmon admitted to being part of the gun store burglary, and acknowledged he handled the firearms after they were taken from the store. Harmon is prohibited from possessing firearms as a result of a prior felony conviction. For the theft charge, Harmon faces up to five years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and a maximum supervised release term of three years. For the illegal possession of a firearm charge, Harmon faces up to 15 years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and a maximum supervised release term of three years. He will be sentenced after the completion of a presentence investigative report by the U.S. Probation Office. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case with the assistance of the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office, the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office, and the Norway Police Department. Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN). ### Contact Peter I. title: Lancaster man arrested, charged with production and possession of child pornography
body: Press Release Lancaster man arrested, charged with production and possession of child pornography Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of New York BUFFALO, N.Y. - U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Jeremy Probst, 33, of Lancaster, NY, was arrested and charged by criminal complaint with production and possession of child pornography, which carry a mandatory minimum penalty of 15 years in prison, a maximum of 30 years, and a $250,000 fine. According to the criminal complaint, in August 2026, Lancaster Police and Homeland Security Investigations received a report of a camera located inside the bathroom of a Lancaster residence associated with Probst. Investigators seized the camera and Probst’s cell phone. A forensic analysis recovered approximately 267 image files and 26 video files containing suspected child pornography from the cell phone. Some of the images were of minor victims known to law enforcement. Also on the cell phone, investigators recovered conversations from the Telegram application between Probst and various Telegram users during which messages were sent indicative of the purchase and sale of suspected child pornography. Probst made an initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Jeremiah J. McCarthy and was held pending a detention hearing on November 20, 2026. If you have any information regarding this defendant, please call Homeland Security Investigations at 716-464-5939. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Aaron J. Mango. The complaint is the result of an investigation by the Lancaster Police Department, under the direction of Chief William Gummo and Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Patrone. The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. # # # # Contact Barbara Burns 716-843-5817 Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - New York, Western

body: Press Release Charlottesville Man Who Broke Courthouse Door, Threated Government Officials Sentenced to 15 Months in Federal Prison Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Virginia CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va. – A local man, who broke the front door of the federal courthouse in Charlottesville and threatened numerous government officials, was sentenced this week to 15 months in federal prison. Joseph Edward Duva, 35, of Charlottesville, previously pled guilty to destruction of public property. In addition, he made threats against the lives of various federal officials that the Court considered as part of its sentencing determination. According to court documents, on February 8, 2026, Duva approached the federal courthouse in Charlottesville with an object and broke the front glass. He later sent a letter, while incarcerated on other charges, admitting to breaking the glass. Duva later sent a series of letters to the United States Attorney’s Office threatening an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA), the then-Acting United States Attorney, and the President of the United States. In addition, on October 9, 2026, the United States Attorney’s Office received a letter addressed to the AUSA who was previously threatened that contained a weapon fashioned from pencils, a toilet paper roll, and latex gloves. The case was investigated by U.S. Marshals Service and the Federal Protective Service First Assistant United States Attorney Robert N. Tracci and Matt Davis, Acting U.S. Marshal for the Western District of Virginia made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sean Welsh prosecuted the case. body: Press Release Knox Place Traffickers Sentenced in Narcotics Conspiracy that Reached from Southern California to Southeast D.C. Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia WASHINGTON – Reginald Lassiter, 40, of the District of Columbia; Terrance Lynwood Boyd, 44, of Capitol Heights, Maryland; and Michael Anderson Thomas, 50, of Chino, California, were sentenced in U.S. District Court in connection with their roles in a drug trafficking organization that distributed fentanyl, PCP, heroin, and cocaine in Southeast Washington, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. “This conspiracy crossed neighborhoods, state lines, and every boundary the defendants thought would shield them from accountability,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “From a California shell company used to funnel drug proceeds, to stash houses in Baltimore, to the streets of Southeast Washington, every piece of the operation left evidence behind. This case sends a clear message: those who flood our streets with dangerous drugs will be held accountable, prosecuted, and sent to prison.” Lassiter, aka "Lip," pleaded guilty on June 17 before U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly to conspiracy to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl. On November 10, Judge Kelly sentenced Lassister to a 120-month prison term and ordered Lassiter to serve five years of supervised release. Boyd pleaded guilty on June 12, 2026, before Judge Kelly to possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense. On November 17, Judge Kelly sentenced Boyd to a 60-month prison term and ordered Boyd to serve five years of supervised release. Thomas pleaded guilty on July 22, 2026, before Judge Kelly to conspiracy to distribute one kilogram or more of phencyclidine (PCP) and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. On November 19, Judge Kelly sentenced Thomas to 195 months in prison and ordered him to serve five years of supervised release. According to court documents, in the summer of 2024, FBI agents initiated a long-term investigation of a drug trafficking conspiracy centered around the 2900 block of Knox Place, SE. Law enforcement had identified an alleged fentanyl and PCP trafficker in the 2900 block of Knox Place. As the investigation progressed, law enforcement identified upstream sources of supply for both narcotics, including California-based co-conspirators such as Thomas. During the conspiracy, five homicides, seventeen assaults with dangerous weapons, five robberies and eight burglaries occurred within 1,000 feet of the conspiracy's primary stash location on Knox Place SE, court papers state. The investigation culminated in August 2025 when law enforcement executed 20 residential search warrants across the District of Columbia, Maryland, and Los Angeles and arrested fourteen individuals. Investigators seized 20 firearms, large quantities of fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and PCP, a kilo press used to compact narcotics, and more than $100,000 in cash. Lassiter operated as a fentanyl supplier within the conspiracy. He served as an intermediary between the conspiracy’s Baltimore-based bulk fentanyl supplier, Thomas Hancock, and the street-level supplier in the 2900 block of Knox Place, co-defendant Eric Prather. Lassiter and Prather maintained a stash house within the 2900 block of Knox Place, which they used to both store and distribute fentanyl and other narcotics. The lavender-hued fentanyl called “purple rain,” that Lassiter supplied to a co-conspirator Feb. 11, 2025. Boyd possessed firearms in furtherance of the organization's drug trafficking activities. During a Aug. 26, 2025, search of a residence on the 2900 block of Knox Place SE, agents recovered a Draco-style firearm from a backpack stashed inside a bedroom closet. Nearby, they recovered distribution quantities of fentanyl, PCP, and heroin. DNA analysis linked Boyd to the firearm. Later that day, agents searched Boyd's residence in the 1200 block of Southern Avenue SE, where they recovered more than $10,000 in cash and a loaded Ruger 5.7 pistol. During a Aug. 26, 2025, search of a residence on the 2900 block of Knox Place SE agents recovered a Draco-style firearm from a backpack stashed inside a bedroom closet. Nearby, they recovered distribution quantities of fentanyl, PCP, and heroin. Thomas facilitated bulk shipments of PCP to co-conspirators operating in the Baltimore-Washington region from his operating base in Chino, California. In late-2024, he agreed to ship 17 gallons of PCP to Hancock. To accept payments for his drug trafficking, Thomas created a California shell company, Never to Late Shipping LLC. Between August 2024 and March 2025, he accepted about $170,000 through the company in connection with the PCP transaction with Hancock. In March 2025, Thomas’ business partner, Darrell Smith, was stopped by Kansas state police outside of Topeka. Kansas state police subsequently conducted a search of Smith’s Dodge Ram and found approximately 17 gallons of PCP concealed within a black lockbox in the truck bed. The PCP was packaged in 17 one-gallon cans that were each sealed. The PCP was packaged in 17 sealed one-gallon cans. Approximately five months later, Thomas’ residence in Chino, California, was searched as part of the coordinated search and arrest operation in this case. In the rear of the residence, a standalone backyard shed serving as a clandestine PCP laboratory was located, containing chemical production materials, multiple large-capacity trash bins and other paraphernalia, including a Senior Master Can Sealer Model 1502. Law enforcement separately located $26,000 in cash and two loaded handguns within the residence, each of which Thomas admitted to possessing. Investigators uncovered a clandestine PCP lab in a shed in Thomas’ backyard in Chino, California. The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office, with valuable assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration, Washington Division Office, and the Metropolitan Police Department. The matter was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Matthew W. Kinskey and John Crabb, Jr., of the Violent Crime and Narcotics Trafficking Section. This operation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by President Trump’s Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Washington D.C. comprises agents and officers from the FBI, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Drug Enforcement Administration, Homeland Security Investigations, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, IRS Criminal Investigations and others with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. 25cr241 25cr273 Follow us on X , Instagram , and YouTube Or at https://www.justice.gov/usao-dc Updated November 19, 2026 Topics Homeland Security Task Force Drug Trafficking Components Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - District of Columbia

title: Former Sheriff’s Deputy, Wife Admit Trying to Coerce Teen into Sexual Activity
body: Press Release Former Sheriff’s Deputy, Wife Admit Trying to Coerce Teen into Sexual Activity Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Missouri ST. LOUIS – A former deputy sheriff and his wife, a former 911 dispatcher, have admitted trying to coerce a child into engaging in sexual activity. David Blankenship, 41, of St. Francois County, pleaded guilty Thursday in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of attempted coercion and enticement of a child. His wife, Karlie Blankenship, 31, pleaded guilty in August to the same charge. The couple both admitted spending months planning how to get an 11-year-old to engage in sex with them. In TikTok and Facebook exchanges beginning in February 2024, the two discussed their desire to meet and have sexual relationships with underage girls. David Blankenship sent his wife pictures of local girls that he’d found online and told her to connect with them. He suggested exchanging drugs for sex with them. The couple also discussed producing and selling pornography online. When their attention turned to the 11-year-old, David Blankenship discussed drugging her with muscle relaxers or hallucinogenic mushrooms and bought her a sex toy. Karlie Blankenship showed the victim images of teenage girls in erotic clothing to gauge her interest. The investigation began when the Missouri State Highway Patrol received a CyberTip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) about the uploading of files that contained suspected child sexual abuse material, and a warning that the suspect "may be law enforcement at St. Francois County Sheriff’s Department and may have current ACCESS TO CHILDREN." Investigators then uncovered the social media communications. When they conducted a court-approved search of the Blankenship home, they found the sex toy, mushrooms in a bag in the Blankenships’ bedroom and methamphetamine in the pocket of a pair of pants worn by David Blankenship. David Blankenship’s employment with the St. Francois County Sheriff’s Department was terminated when his department learned of the allegations. Karlie Blankenship is scheduled to be sentenced on December 1 and David Blankenship on February 17. The charge carries a mandatory minimum prison term of 10 years and a maximum term of life. The Missouri State Highway Patrol, the Missouri State Technical Assistance Team and the St. Francois County Sheriff’s Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Hayes is prosecuting the case. Contact Robert Patrick, Public Affairs Officer, robert.patrick@usdoj.gov. Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Missouri, Eastern

Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Cyber resilience guidance consultation and AI and quantum effective practices UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. Published on  
        19 November 2026 News release UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. The Bank of England’s (the Bank) latest Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in 5 years, 52% above the previous 18-month peak recorded in May 2025. In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them. The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast evolving threat environment. It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers. Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: 'Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance. 'Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.' Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said: 'Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.' Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said: 'We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents. 'The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.' Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area. Notes to editors The consultation closes on 26 February 2027. Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year. The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements. The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve. The proposed guidance covers key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas including: - Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management , with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate Board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance. - Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk , maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts. - Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats , applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains. - Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly , through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks. - Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively , with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned. The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future. See Effective practices: Cyber risk and resilience management relating to artificial intelligence (AI) and Effective practices: Cyber risk and resilience management relating to quantum computing . A recent Bank of England and FCA survey , found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years. In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI. Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Minutes of the Market Participants Group meeting – 18 November 2026 The Market Participants Group (MPG) is a senior-level forum for financial market participants to share their views on relevant themes and narratives in financial markets with members of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee. Published on  
        19 November 2026 Time: 5pm – 6.30pm | Location: Bank of England Published on 19 November 2026 Minutes Item 1 – Welcome The Governor began the meeting by thanking attendees for joining and reminding participants of the purpose of these meetings. The Governor made clear that the MPC would be in listening mode, and that the meeting would be conducted in accordance with relevant competition and conduct laws, as per the terms of reference . Item 2 – International developments Market participants opened by discussing developments in major advanced economies outside the UK. The resilience of global growth and the strength of corporate sector balance sheets, particularly in the United States, were noted. Energy markets were also discussed, with market participants highlighting the inherent difficulty of forecasting energy prices amid continued geopolitical uncertainty. The material support to global growth from AI-related capital expenditure was noted. Participants also discussed the increasing role of debt financing and the potential implications of a change in expectations around AI for risky asset markets, investment and consumption. The discussion also covered potential financial market vulnerabilities arising from elevated hedge-fund leverage, sovereign debt pressures and cyber risks. Item 3 – Domestic developments Market participants discussed the outlook for the UK economy and the implications for monetary policy. Participants noted the resilience of UK growth this year despite the energy shock. This resilience was broadly seen to have strengthened the case for higher rates, with the November increase having been widely expected. Growth in global AI-related investment was noted as one factor supporting UK activity, although there was some discussion over the extent to which the resilience in domestic growth would persist. Participants also discussed the implications of AI-related growth for domestic inflationary pressure. Market participants noted the correlation between energy prices and market rates, and how this relationship had evolved over recent months. In discussing the implications of the energy shock, views differed on the relative importance of its demand and supply-side effects. The distinction between implied pricing in the market curve and modal expectations for policy was also noted by market participants. body:

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 18, 2026 Investing in America’s Underserved Communities Governor Michael S. Barr At Making Missing Markets: Catalyzing Capital and Igniting Innovation, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York Share Thank you to the New York Fed and the organizers of this conference for the opportunity to speak to you today. 1 For two reasons I can think of, New York is an excellent place to discuss ways to increase investments in communities where incomplete or missing markets have resulted in less investment than needed. First, it makes sense to initiate a conversation about incentivizing private investment in the center of American finance. Second, New York has been successful over the past few decades in attracting investment in lower-income neighborhoods, reversing forces that once made parts of this city synonymous with urban decline. I first saw that for myself 30 years ago, touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public–private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer, block by block. That progress has continued, and the strategies and partnerships we will be discussing today have been a major engine for that success. The backdrop for community investment, of course, is the economy—how fast it is growing, how well it is creating jobs, and how well incomes are keeping up with the cost of living. So I will start with the economic outlook. Overall, the economy is strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment. But inflation is too high, making it hard for American families to make ends meet. Many families are struggling. And that's why it is so important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to our target of 2 percent in a timely way. If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people. Of course, I'll continue to monitor the incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks in making that assessment. Strong and sustainable communities are key to American prosperity. When a community is strong and resilient, people see a future there and invest in that future—they buy homes, shop locally, and start new businesses. When hard times hit resilient communities, people can weather the storm and bounce back in part because they believe that they and their communities will bounce back—that jobs and opportunities will return. That's why we at the Fed are committed to building stronger communities. And while economic activity and employment are continuing to grow for the country as a whole, not all families and communities are thriving. Far from it. Wealthier households are doing well, but middle- and lower-income households are struggling, and the economy is leaving some communities behind. Recent estimates are that 44 percent of Americans live in low-income communities, where a fifth or more of people live below the poverty line. 2 These communities often lack sufficient investment in housing, business, and infrastructure. The Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that the majority of households has very little wealth. 3 And lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say that they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help or provide that help themselves. 4 Think about how that inability to help, or get help, can reverberate across a community. When jobs and opportunities lag in a community, it eats away at the ties that connect families and neighbors. The dignity of work is so key to how many people try to navigate these difficult times, yet in many communities, despite a strong economy, some people are finding it hard to find a good-paying job. So, what are the kinds of investments that can drive long-term, lasting opportunity? We've seen so many examples of successful public–private partnerships make a difference to households, businesses, and communities. We need the public sector, at all levels of government. We need the private sector. And we need the nonprofit sector. But there are market failures that often prevent the private sector from coming in on its own. For example, information asymmetries can make it hard for commercial banks to see opportunities in low-income areas. When commercial banks can partner with local, state, and national community development groups, including Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), that partnership can help those banks extend credit, investment, and services to those that most need them and, in turn, assist banks in most effectively reaching new customers. These partnerships can help overcome these market failures. Community organizations and national nonprofits can reduce the costs of acquiring and interpreting information about low-income borrowers and communities, they can coordinate lending to overcome collective action problems, and they can also share risks to reduce bank exposures. By targeting investments to identify root causes of the challenges in a community, public–private partnerships can better help capital find successful strategies at the early stages of the development process. This can help establish the appropriate funding infrastructure to set community-focused projects on a course for long-term investment. 5 As President John Williams said in inaugurating this conference in 2024, this event is about investing in solutions that lead to long-term partnerships and sustainable success. 6 It means addressing root causes, and also the longer-term outlook for the community. Investments that focus on jobs, housing, schools, infrastructure, and the like are critical. To illustrate what I mean, I will note a few examples of where communities in the region are building partnerships to attract long-term investments. Not far from here, in a part of Brooklyn marked by limited housing as well as a lack of employment and healthy food sources, private and public partners came together in a project called City Point, which includes a full-service supermarket, 120 affordable housing units, and retail space for local small businesses. City Point is a great example of how the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) can leverage private investment into communities and spur further development. 7 I helped launch the bipartisan NMTC a quarter century ago, and I'm so pleased that it was recently made permanent by Congress. In Middletown, New York, the city is converting a historic railway station, long vacant, into a community center, complete with a Head Start program in a community where childcare options are sparse. The project is being financed in part by the NMTC. Syracuse, New York, announced earlier this year the creation of a revolving loan fund for mixed-income housing. The fund provided $30 million in seed money, and a group of private partners contributed the remaining $120 million. The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LITHC) has been a critical tool so important to the recovery of the Bronx and many communities around the country. The LIHTC has helped to create or preserve nearly 4 million units of housing over the past 40 years. 8 The Bronx lost roughly a fifth of its housing between 1970 and 1980 and, not coincidentally, about a fifth of its population. But with the help of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), the LIHTC, CDFIs, and other factors, it recovered that ground and continues to recover and thrive since then. 9 Underpinning all of these projects is the CRA. The CRA has helped to increase lending, investment, and services in low-income communities all across the country. Critical to the CRA's success are banks of all sizes—the biggest banks that serve national markets, regional banks, banks with specialized business models, and community banks—in all kinds of communities, including urban, suburban, small towns, and rural. Banks large and small often partner with CDFIs, national and local community as well as civil rights groups, local chambers of commerce, and the like to make local lending effective. CDFIs are often "boots on the ground" financial providers and can connect stakeholders across sectors. Grants to these and other groups often make the difference between success and failure for banks trying to make a difference in communities—as I said, in rural communities, small towns, big cities, and Native American lands alike. Today, I've spoken mostly about community development in New York, since we're here in the Second District, but I've seen work like this first-hand all around the country as I've visited the Reserve Bank Districts. I've listened to bankers, CDFIs, and local entrepreneurs come together in Clarksdale, Mississippi. I've seen affordable housing built by partnerships between tribal governments and local banks on the Flathead and Blackfeet Reservations in Montana. I've seen Working Cities in East Harford, Connecticut, and community-based learning in Portland, Oregon. I've witnessed the transformation, innovation, and entrepreneurial spirit of Detroit, Michigan, and the grit and determination of community development professionals in South Dallas, Texas. Entrepreneurs in Charlotte, North Carolina, told me about the importance of CDFIs, as did leaders in Kansas City, Missouri, and Omaha, Nebraska. I've seen what public–private partnerships mean for employment and small business growth in Cleveland, Ohio, and I've seen a business incubator in Atlanta, Georgia, make a real difference to its local community. In Arizona, I visited with entrepreneurs in Mesa and Tempe who told us about the key role of local community development corporations. And Chicago educational leaders taught me the importance of linking up with local employers to chart job pathways for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds. This good work is happening all over the country, in urban, rural, and tribal communities, and in every Reserve Bank District. This brings us to why we are gathered today at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In one part of this building, staff are working every day to help implement monetary policy, help ensure smooth financial markets, and promote a strong economy. But we can't achieve a strong economy without strong communities. Core to the Fed's mission, the Federal Reserve System's Community Development function can help. I applaud the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for bringing attention to the untapped potential of low- and moderate-income communities all across these beautiful, vast, diverse, and entrepreneurial United States. There's lots more we can do together. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. body: Google for Mexico: Technology impact that goes beyond business Nov 18, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link At this year’s Google for Mexico, we announced how our latest AI innovations and partnerships are translating into real-world growth across the country. Sebastian Valverde Country Managing Director, Google Mexico Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. You can visit our website to read the full Economic Impact Report and learn more about our ongoing partnerships with local institutions. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Sebastian Valverde reports that Google tools contributed 382 billion pesos to the Mexican economy during 2025. We are partnering with national agencies to provide precise weather alerts for extreme climate events. You can now use the Gemini app on Android devices with low memory across the country. Our new Mexico City office will house over one thousand staff members developing global software products. We provided 1.65 million dollars to UNICEF for digital literacy and online safety programs for children. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Sebastian Valverde, Country Managing Director for Google Mexico, explains how our tools are helping local businesses grow and communities stay safe. We are providing precise weather alerts to help people prepare for storms, and we launched a new version of the Gemini app for simpler phones. These updates help students, business owners, and families across Mexico access helpful technology, learn new skills, and stay safe online. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Nearly a year ago, I arrived in Mexico after leading our operations in Miami, with a very clear mission: to continue making Google the best partner for every entrepreneur, business, institution, and person looking to grow here. I knew I was joining a vibrant ecosystem, but reality far exceeded every expectation. In this time, I’ve discovered a country that refuses to be a bystander to the future; Mexico challenges it, embraces it with remarkable speed, and, above all, builds it with its own hands. Going from promise to everyday action For years, we spoke about artificial intelligence as a scientific marvel or an assistant capable of answering questions. Today, however, we are witnessing a fundamental turning point: AI has evolved from providing answers to taking concrete action. It’s no longer just about drafting an email or summarizing a document; it’s about intelligent agents solving complex, multi-step tasks, freeing up valuable time for what truly matters. And when innovation lands in the real world, results are measured in tangible growth. In our latest Economic Impact Report, we confirmed that Google’s tools contributed over 382 billion Mexican pesos in economic activity across Mexico in 2025. Put into perspective, that’s more than 1 billion pesos flowing through local businesses every single day. Behind that number are the real stories that inspire us: for every peso a business invests in Google Ads, it earns an average of eight pesos in commercial return. Whether it’s the neighborhood fonda managing reservations seamlessly or a company modernizing its operations in the cloud, technology only carries real value when it creates shared prosperity. Solving the challenges that matter together At Google for Mexico 2026, we reaffirmed that this potential goes far beyond business. For example, it can help us tackle urgent challenges like climate change and hurricane seasons. Google’s cutting-edge science can provide weather prediction hour by hour, and with up to 15 days in advance. We put that technology to work, partnering closely with the National Water Commission ( CONAGUA ) and the National Meteorological Service to support the forecast for extreme weather events and deliver more precise real-time alerts directly to people’s phones. At the same time, access must never be a luxury. That’s why we are launching the Gemini app for lower memory Android devices in Mexico, redesigned to run smoothly on phones with as little as 2 GB of RAM. Millions of students and local business owners now have access to guided tutoring, voice interaction, and creative assistance in the palm of their hands. And because the future belongs to the next generation, Google.org contributed with $1.65 million in funding to UNICEF to support digital literacy and online safety programmes for children and adolescents across Latin America. In Mexico, UNICEF will use this support to reach more than 300,000 parents, caregivers, teachers and students with practical tools to help prevent and identify online risks early. Building from Mexico for the world Coming soon, we will open our new offices in Mexico City, bringing more than a thousand Googlers together under one roof. Among them are world-class Mexican software engineers already developing global products like Google Chrome. Mexico no longer just uses technology; it creates it, transforms it, and projects it to the world. Being part of this journey is an immense privilege. Let’s keep building a future where technology is, above all, a bridge so that no one is left behind. title: Introducing Stitch Loop: A new way to build and evolve products
body: Introducing Stitch Loop: A new way to build and evolve products Nov 18, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link As part of a new direction for Stitch, we’re introducing a new experiment, Stitch Loop: a long-running product agent that connects to your codebase and live metrics to continuously improve what you’ve shipped. Justin Toupin Director, Product Management, Google Labs Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We are introducing Stitch Loop, a product agent that connects to your codebase and live metrics to continuously optimize your software. It identifies issues, suggests fixes, and opens pull requests to help your team maintain product quality around the clock. You can join the waitlist today at stitch.google.com/loop/waitlist to get started with these automated tools for security, latency, and accessibility. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Justin Toupin introduces Stitch Loop, a product agent that monitors your codebase and metrics continuously. This tool identifies areas for improvement, writes code in a sandbox, and submits pull requests. You maintain full control over all changes because you must approve every pull request manually. The system includes dedicated loops for cybersecurity, latency, and accessibility to help your lean team. You can join the global waitlist today to receive priority access for your development projects. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are introducing Stitch Loop, a new tool from Google Labs that helps you maintain and improve your software after it launches. It connects to your code and live data to find bugs, fix security issues, and boost performance around the clock. You simply review the suggested changes before they go live. This helps your team focus on building new features while the agent handles the ongoing work of keeping your product running well. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Coding agents let you build and ship new features fast, but their job ends the moment your pull request merges. Once code hits production, the real work starts: patching vulnerabilities, speeding up checkout, and diagnosing signup drop-offs buried in noisy feedback. For lean teams, balancing post-launch maintenance with continuous improvement is a constant challenge, yet it’s also what drives some of the world’s most successful products. Today, we are introducing Stitch Loop, a long-running product agent from Google Labs that connects to your codebase and live metrics, finds what needs fixing, and keeps working 24/7 on your product until your goals are met. Millions of designers, developers, and founders already use Stitch to turn ideas into working interfaces in minutes. Together, Stitch and Stitch Loop are steps toward our broader ambition for Stitch: creating agents to help lean teams tackle the hardest parts of creating great products from ideation through continuous optimization. See how it works You start by connecting GitHub and your product context (logs, user behavior, feedback, etc) with over 180 integrations, custom MCP servers, or local CLI uploads. Grounded in that context, Stitch Loop runs evergreen loops to continuously optimize toward the measurable outcomes you care about. You get three default loops out of the box and can add your own anytime. Each loop runs through four steps: Suggestions: Stitch Loop surfaces opportunities to make progress towards your goals, grounded in evidence from your product. Solutions: Every suggestion comes with one or more solutions— each with tradeoffs and scoping, along with visual design options where applicable. Build: Once you choose a direction, Stitch Loop writes the code in an isolated cloud sandbox and opens a GitHub pull request for your approval. When relevant, the PR will contain screenshots and videos of the work Loop did. Reflect: Stitch Loop monitors live product data as it works toward your goal, learning from every positive or negative result to sharpen the next round of insights. Once the goal is met, it keeps watching in case the metric slips. You always have the final call. Nothing merges until you review the PR. Automate codebase security Stitch Loop comes with built-in loops for cybersecurity, latency, and accessibility, plus the ability to create custom loops like improving checkout conversion. Security is often the hardest gap to cover for lean teams shipping quickly. Stitch Loop includes a dedicated security loop that pairs Gemini 4 Carbon's cyber security capabilities with CodeMender , Google DeepMind's autonomous agent that improves code security. Together, they scan your codebase for security vulnerabilities before they become incidents. Stitch Loop flags each issue it finds with evidence and opens a PR with a proposed fix for your review. Use it with your agents and existing workflows You can use Stitch Loop as a service layer for coding agents, like Google Antigravity, or bring it into the places where your team already works, like Slack. Whatever coding agent you prefer can pull persistent product context from Stitch Loop via the Stitch CLI and MCP to power mixed-model setups and fully autonomous improvements in your existing workflow. In Slack, just use @stitch to get daily insight digests and create new loops. Join the waitlist The Stitch Loop waitlist opens today for all users, globally, with eligible Google AI Ultra users getting priority access. Join at stitch.google.com/loop/waitlist and share your feedback in the Google Labs Discord . Get the latest news from Google in your inbox Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription. You can also subscribe with a different email address . Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. title: The Gemini app is now available on lower-memory Android devices.
body: The Gemini app is now available on lower-memory Android devices. Angus Logan Builder, Gemini App Nov 18, 2026 For hundreds of millions of people globally, a lower-memory Android device is their everyday connection to the internet, education, and business. Until recently, hardware limits meant those phones only had basic voice commands. Now, we’re bringing the Gemini app to eligible Android (Go edition) devices , putting Google’s personal AI assistant in the hands of hundreds of millions more people. We re-architected the app so the core Gemini experience runs smoothly on hardware with less memory. Instead of typing out long prompts, you can talk things through or practice for an interview out loud in more than 45 languages with Gemini Live , point your camera at notes or forms to learn and translate, or create custom images with Nano Banana — like a flyer for a weekend bakery sale. To get started, download the Gemini app on Google Play, press and hold the power button on supported phones, or look for it preloaded on upcoming devices from partners like Transsion.
retained_feed_body: The Google Gemini app now supports lower-memory Android devices. Access Gemini Live and custom image creation on your phone. Download the app today.

title: Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025
body: News Release Explore Product View News Release Related Materials Contacts EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 10:00 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 18, 2026 BEA 26–48 Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025 New Statistics for 2025; Updates for 2021–2024 Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1). Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9). Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama ( BEA interactive tables ). Outdoor recreation by activity Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024. Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2): Boating/fishing was the largest conventional activity for the nation at $39.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 35 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($4.5 billion), California ($3.3 billion), and Texas ($3.0 billion). RVing was the second-largest conventional activity for the nation at $26.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 10 states. The states with the largest contributions were Indiana ($4.7 billion), Texas ($2.6 billion), and California ($2.1 billion). Hunting/shooting/trapping was the third-largest conventional activity for the nation at $15.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Arizona and Wyoming. The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($1.8 billion), California ($849.8 million), and Florida ($831.3 million). Snow activities for the nation totaled $7.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Colorado, Utah, and Vermont. The states with the largest contributions were Colorado ($1.8 billion), California ($735.7 million), and Utah ($640.1 million). Outdoor recreation by industry The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation. For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3). Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion). Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion). Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data. Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive . For definitions, statistical conventions, BEA regions, uses of these statistics, and more, visit " Additional Information " Next release: Fall 2027 Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2026 Full Release & Tables PDF Tables - National Level XLSX Tables - State Level XLSX Interactive State Tables Additional Information Technical Stanislaw Rzeznik (Regional) 301-278-9458 OutdoorRecreation@bea.gov Technical Connor Franks (National) 301‐278‐9710 OutdoorRecreation@bea.gov Media Connie O'Connell 301-278-9003 Connie.OConnell@bea.gov

Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia.

title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
body: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now Systems from ASUS, Dell and MSI are now available — with more from Acer, GIGABYTE, HP and Microsoft on the way — bringing RTX acceleration and up to 128GB of unified memory to local AI, development and creative workflows. November 18, 2026 by Justin Walker 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. A Windows PC Built for Local AI As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops like the ASUS ProArt GR1X mini PC are built to run personal AI agents 24/7. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ Series RTX Spark compact desktop. New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . From Local Agents to AI Creation Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark. Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark. Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting. GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables. Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark. Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work. The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time. DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software. Windows Server 2028 Coming to DGX Station for Windows Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data. Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip is expanding to include support for Windows Server 2028. New accelerator platforms and the breadth of the Windows silicon ecosystem provide customers options at different capability levels and price points for advanced AI development, local inference, and agent workloads at scale. Windows ML Updates Give Developers More Options Also announced at Microsoft Ignite, developers can now bring any GGUF model from Hugging Face and run it within Windows ML using the llama.cpp backend. The DxCGC backend, now available as an experimental release, is an integration for game developers that compiles and runs machine learning models through DirectX 12, allowing them to execute AI workloads alongside graphics. Windows APIs let applications integrate platform-provided AI capabilities adding GPU support for AION Instruct and VSR. Developers can also build high-performance AI models for Windows ML using the command line interface. #ICYMI: The Latest NVIDIA Local AI Updates 🦙 llama.cpp v1.0.0 marks a major milestone for building local AI apps. The open source inference engine introduces API versioning updates, alongside expanded model support and CUDA optimizations for NVFP4 inference. Learn more . 🎉 Ricursive Intelligence introduced its first open model: Ripple-65B Preview. The full-stack AI lab builds self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software and models. Ripple-65B Preview was trained on NVIDIA B300 GPUs, refined using NVIDIA Nemotron post-training datasets and runs locally on DGX Spark. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face . 🤖 Runway’s Praxis-1 is a newly released 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and actions together. Developers can run it locally on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, DGX Spark and DGX Station, and adapt it to their own robots, cameras and tasks with LoRA fine-tuning. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face . 🛠️ NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM helps run AI models locally on DGX Spark with just a few commands. Read the technical blog , which walks through downloading Nemotron-3.5 Lightning, setting up optimized inference, testing prompts and serving the model through a local OpenAI-compatible API. Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information.
